research_text:
## Research brief

### 1. What the finding refers to

`java.security.MessageDigest` provides message-digest algorithms: it processes data and produces a fixed-length hash. The reported `InvalidSequenceOfMethodCalls` message concerns the **order of modeled calls on a digest object**, not, by itself, a particular algorithm value or the contents of the digest. A sequence failure is distinct from a violation of the rule’s algorithm constraint. The supplied message does not identify the refused call or provide a complete trace. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))

The published CrySL rule requires acquisition followed by one or more modeled digest-computation branches. A direct `digest(byte[])` is one such branch. The published rule also allows one or more `update` calls followed by **any** modeled `digest` overload, including `digest(byte[])`. Thus, the narrower protocol in the supplied description is not identical to the published rule. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))

### 2. Documented usage and remediation guidance

Oracle documents an initialized object obtained through `getInstance`; data can be supplied through `update`, then completed with `digest`. `digest(byte[])` performs a final update and completes the computation. After completion, the object resets; `reset()` can also be called explicitly. These are JDK API semantics, which are not identical to the CrySL rule’s more restrictive modeled order. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))

Oracle’s API documentation does **not** prescribe a universal remediation for a reported sequence violation. For algorithm selection, Oracle says applications must determine whether an algorithm meets their security requirements. NIST recommends transitioning away from SHA-1 for cryptographic protection by December 31, 2030, while recognizing a possible need to process previously protected information afterward. That guidance does not classify a particular digest use. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html?utm_source=openai))

A digest comparison alone does not establish authentication. For requirements involving authentication or keyed integrity, Oracle separately documents `Mac`, including HMAC with a shared secret; `Signature` provides digital-signature functionality. These are different APIs and contracts, not automatic substitutes for every digest use. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/Mac.html))

### 3. Compatibility and migration

- **Outputs and formats:** Oracle specifies SHA-1 as 160 bits and SHA-256 as 256 bits. Changing algorithms therefore changes the digest representation and can affect stored identifiers or wire fields that require the old value. The API documentation does not define a general persisted-format or wire-format migration. Whether an external contract permits a change remains unresolved. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html?utm_source=openai))
- **Platform support:** Java SE 21’s `MessageDigest` documentation requires SHA-1 and SHA-256 support, but directs users to implementation documentation for other algorithms. Java SE 26 additionally lists SHA-384 as required. Provider and target-version support must therefore be checked; the rule’s allowance of SHA-512 is not itself a platform-support guarantee. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html))
- **Migration path:** NIST’s SHA-1 transition notice acknowledges legacy protected information, but neither it nor the examined `MessageDigest` API documentation specifies a migration for a particular cache, persisted identifier, runtime discriminator, or wire protocol. ([csrc.nist.gov](https://csrc.nist.gov/news/2022/nist-transitioning-away-from-sha-1-for-all-apps?utm_source=openai))

### 4. Exact published CrySL matching rule

The following clauses are verbatim from the specified `MessageDigest.crysl` source: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))

```text
SPEC java.security.MessageDigest

g1: getInstance(algorithm);
g2: getInstance(algorithm, _);
Get := g1 | g2;

ORDER
    Get, (DWOU | (Update+, Digest))+

CONSTRAINTS
    algorithm in {"SHA-256", "SHA-384", "SHA-512"};
```

The source declares `algorithm` as `java.lang.String`. It models `getInstance` with one argument or two arguments, the second represented by `_`; it also models the listed `update` and `digest` forms with their declared parameter types and counts. Its order condition is shown above, and its additional constraints govern array lengths, offsets, and positive lengths. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))

**A method on an unrelated type that merely shares one of these names is not what this rule specifies:** the rule declares `SPEC java.security.MessageDigest`, rather than a name-only, all-types match. The file itself does not document a particular scanner’s type-resolution or subclass-matching implementation. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl))

### Sources and limits

- Published CrySL rule: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/MessageDigest.crysl
- Oracle Java SE 21 API: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html
- Oracle Java SE 26 API: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/MessageDigest.html
- Oracle standard algorithm names: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html
- NIST SHA-1 transition notice: https://csrc.nist.gov/news/2022/nist-transitioning-away-from-sha-1-for-all-apps

The CrySL URL is a moving `master` branch. The supplied SHA-256 value was not independently verified against the rule revision bundled with the detector. The refused event, resolved call target, algorithm value, runtime reachability, digest purpose, and any external format contract remain unspecified.
